title: The West Has a Crisis of Hope
gist: Former Estonian president Kersti Kaljulaid argues Western protests reflect intergenerational hopelessness from a shrinking labor share of GDP, housing-driven wealth accumulation, and a low-wage-plus-welfare model that subsidizes employers. She proposes pay covering full labor costs, lower business taxes, falling social support and equal taxation of all income.

insights.claim: The labor share of GDP in OECD countries peaked around 70 percent in the 1970s and fell to between 50 and 60 percent by the 2000s, meaning ordinary citizens get a smaller slice of output.
insights.speaker: Kersti Kaljulaid
insights.so_what: A falling labor share underpins consumer weakness, populism and political risk across developed markets.
insights.quote: Put simply, ordinary citizens in rich societies are getting a smaller portion of the total economic pie.
insights.locator: As young people take to the streets

insights.claim: Rising wealth accumulates mostly in residential real estate, so younger generations who cannot climb the housing ladder see salaries minus rent yield mediocre prospects and greater dependence on social security.
insights.speaker: Kersti Kaljulaid
insights.so_what: Housing-driven wealth inequality fuels generational resentment and political instability; supports a view of structurally weak young-cohort demand.
insights.locator: A key feature of this problem

insights.claim: Compared with the 1980s, when labor compensation was about 70 percent of GDP with social spending near 16 percent and deficits near 2 percent, today workers get less, social spending is much higher and deficits are almost double.
insights.speaker: Kersti Kaljulaid
insights.so_what: Fiscal pressure from welfare spending and thin wage share limits government capacity; relevant for sovereign debt dynamics.
insights.locator: The results are plain to see

themes.theme: Low wages subsidized by the state

insights.claim: Businesses have pushed labor costs onto social budgets by lobbying for low or unfixed minimum wages, so state support spread from the underskilled to skilled workers, including teachers, nurses and police in wealthy areas.
insights.speaker: Kersti Kaljulaid
insights.so_what: Employer reliance on welfare top-ups is a hidden subsidy and a fiscal vulnerability when tax bases shrink.
insights.locator: Initially, this state support was necessary

insights.claim: The system is a downward spiral because government revenue depends on middle-class wages: suppressed wage growth lowers tax revenue, which lowers public-sector salaries and raises demand for support.
insights.speaker: Kersti Kaljulaid
insights.so_what: A self-reinforcing fiscal-wage loop implies chronic deficits unless wages rise.
insights.locator: All of this results in a downward spiral

insights.claim: Kaljulaid proposes that salaries cover the full regional cost of labor, offset by lower business taxes and gradually reduced social support, with the EU and OECD publishing methodology for localized labor values.
insights.speaker: Kersti Kaljulaid
insights.so_what: A policy direction that would raise wages while cutting employer taxes; watch for EU-level debate on adequate wages.

insights.claim: All income, whether salaries, dividends or rents, should be taxed similarly, because independent workers enjoy corporate tax models that salaried individuals do not.
insights.speaker: Kersti Kaljulaid
insights.so_what: Would raise taxes on capital and self-employed income relative to wages; a possible tax-policy direction.
insights.locator: Part of the puzzle will be figuring out

insights.claim: AI could hurt job growth but could also raise productivity and salaries if rolled out with attention to distribution, while growing independent and remote work raises workers' bargaining power over businesses.
insights.speaker: Kersti Kaljulaid
insights.so_what: Outcome depends on policy design; treat as an open question rather than a forecast.
insights.locator: But this traditional hold is weakening

insights.claim: Intergenerational hopelessness breeds revolutions, as people with little to lose want to break a system that failed them even when they doubt populist or extremist proposals will work, which would impede progress on collective problems like climate change.
insights.speaker: Kersti Kaljulaid
insights.so_what: Raises the probability of protest-driven political shocks and populist victories across Europe.
insights.locator: The risk of inaction is clear
